title: Technical deep dive - autoscaling & capacity planning
summary: Deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning for Redwood runtime. Covered burst policies, reserved GPU pools, queueing/latency models, KV cache warmup, batching tradeoffs, quantization impacts, and private VPC deployment constraints. Agreed to run a pilot benchmark, share capacity template and cost modelling, and follow up with a POC timeline.
action_items: Jordan Blake: Send capacity planning template, sample cost model, and pricing sheet by 2026-03-06
Samira Khan: Share recent 8k-token benchmark results (A100 vs H100) and recommended quantization profiles by 2026-03-05
Ethan Park: Provide peak QPS and 99th latency SLOs + sample traffic trace by 2026-03-05
Priya Desai: Confirm VPC egress constraints and KMS requirements by 2026-03-08
next_steps: Schedule POC kickoff (2 week window) - Jordan to propose calendar options

transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-03-03
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~62 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Blake (Redwood AE), Samira Khan (Redwood SE), Ethan Park (CTO - CloudScale), Priya Desai (Infra Lead), Liam O'Connor (SRE)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): Deep dive on autoscaling and capacity planning: Jordan opened with high-level product framing; Samira went into runtime details. Customer asked lots of infra questions re: reserved GPUs, burst policies, queueing, and KV cache warmup. Conversation touched on quantization and VPC/on-prem considerations.

[00:00] Jordan: ok hi everyone thanks for joining, i'm jordan from redwood, with samira our se. can you hear us?
[00:12] Ethan: yep, all good thanks. quick context, we're evaluating inference for our analytics agents, expect spikes during monthly reports, also some realtime queries.
[00:30] Samira: perfect, today we'll cover autoscaling patterns, reserved capacity, burst policies, how queueing impacts p99, and some tactical notes on kv cache and batching.
[01:05] Priya: our main constraints are: we must keep p99 under 500ms for interactive queries, have strict data residency - private vpc, and want predictable cost for budgeting.
[01:30] Jordan: great, those are super helpful. can you share current qps profile? average vs peak?
[01:42] Ethan: avg about 30 qps, peaks to ~1.2k qps for 10-15 minutes on report runs, then tails off. most requests are short prompts, 512 tokens or less, but a small subset are long context 4-8k tokens.
[02:10] Samira: this mix's important because kv cache warmup for the long-contexts can add latency on first hits; caching and prefix reuse matter. for autoscaling we recommend reserved gpus sized for baseline, plus burst pools.
[02:45] Liam: clarify reserved gpus - you mean dedicated capacity we reserve in a pool? how fast can we scale beyond that?
[02:58] Samira: yes reserved = dedicated gpu pool (redwood dedicated). baseline set to handle steady-state throughput w/ small headroom. for bursts we have two levers: short-term burst capacity (we can pre-warm instances or leverage a shared burst fleet) and queueing with prioritized lanes. scaling to new gpu instances (cold start) can be minutes, so we avoid relying on that for tight p99s.
[03:35] Ethan: so for that 1.2k qps 15-minute spike, what's the recommended approach?
[03:45] Samira: recommended: size reserved to handle, say, 60-70% of expected peak, and configure burst pool to absorb sudden spikes. we can pre-warm nvme-backed kv cache on burst nodes if we know the spike window, or use intelligent prefix caching to reduce warmups. also adaptive batching helps but increases latency for single-request tail.
[04:12] Jordan: important tradeoff: batching reduces tokens/second cost but can add ~20-150ms depending on batch window. we tune to meet p99.
[04:30] Priya: can you explain queueing model? we can't have infinite queues for SLA reasons.
[04:40] Samira: sure. we support prioritized queues: realtime lane with tight timeout and direct routing to warm instances (higher cost), and bulk lane with longer tail latency and batching. bursting uses token bucket rate policies to smooth ingress; when burst capacity exhausted, lower-priority requests go to bulk lane or get 429s based on policy. you set queue depth and backpressure thresholds.
[05:20] Ethan: how do you model p99 when there's mixed long-context and short requests?
[05:30] Samira: simulate with weighted traffic traces - p99 is sensitive to long-context because they tie up GPU for more tokens and their kv cache miss penalty. we model expected service time per request type and run M/G/k queue simulations; practical rule: cap concurrent long-contexts per GPU and reserve nodes specifically for them if they're mission critical.
[06:10] Liam: about kv cache: how long to warm on cold start and how much memory does kv cache use per token? we have large prompts.
[06:22] Samira: warm time depends on model size and sequence length; for big models and 8k contexts first pass can be 500-800ms extra. kv cache memory is roughly O(seq_len * hidden_size) but exact depends on quantization kernel. with quantized weights we still need full-precision keys in many kernels; we recommend using smaller kv-optimized instances or pinning long-context workloads to dedicated nodes.
[07:05] Jordan: also note that prefix/KV caching can be shared across requests for same user session which amortizes cost. if your app has common prefixes we can cache and reuse.
[07:20] Ethan: ok, what about quantization? we thought moving to int8 would save cost but worried about latency and quality.
[07:30] Samira: int8/4-bit quant reduces memory and can increase throughput, but some attention kernels degrade quality. for many open models we validate quant profiles: 8-bit works for embeddings/generation with negligible quality drop for our benchmarks; 4-bit sometimes needs more evals. important: quantized kernels can be faster per-token, but kv cache layouts differ and may increase warmup cost. we'll share our quantization recommendations per model.
[08:10] Priya: VPC/on-prem notes: can the private deployment do the same burst pooling? we have strict egress and cannot use shared cloud burst.
[08:25] Samira: for private, burst pooling is constrained to what you deploy; we can provision secondary reserved nodes for bursts inside your VPC, or enable scheduled pre-warm windows. if you can't expand network egress, we do in-VPC autoscaling only and recommend slightly larger reserved baseline or a predictable scheduled scale during known windows.
[09:00] Jordan: we often recommend hybrid: reserved for baseline in VPC + a small windowed burst contract for scheduled events if compliant.
[09:10] Ethan: pricing for reserved vs burst? how to model cost per peak minute?
[09:20] Jordan: cost model: reserved = hourly committed cost (discounted), burst = on-demand rate. compute effective cost per 1k token by combining baseline amortized reserved cost + on-demand for overflow. we will send a spreadsheet sample.
[09:55] Samira: also watch utilization - overprovisioning reserved capacity wastes money; underprovisioning harms p99. our capacity template helps pick sweet spot given your traffic trace.
[10:20] Liam: about queueing timeouts - if we send a lot of retries we may exacerbate spikes. suggestions?
[10:32] Samira: implement client-side jittered retries and respect 429 backoff headers. on server side we support request shaping and circuit-breakers. prefer failing fast for bulk ops.
[11:05] Ethan: curious about metrics you expose to monitor autoscaling effectiveness?
[11:12] Jordan: console offers per-route token/sec, GPU utilization, queue depth by lane, cold-start rate, kv cache hit ratio, and p50/p95/p99 latencies. we can add custom traces as needed.
[12:00] Priya: on private deployment, will observability be identical? we need audit logs and KMS integration.
[12:12] Samira: yes, private deployment includes same telemetry to your console instance, audit logs forwarded to your SIEM, and KMS/HSM support for keys. we can redact user data per policy.
[12:45] Ethan: will latency to several regions matter? our users are global but most traffic in NA.
[12:53] Jordan: route by region: keep warm instances in region, failover to nearest region with slightly higher latency. automatic fallback to smaller models if capacity constrained is supported.
[13:25] Samira: quick note on model variants: we support model families and quantized variants; fallback policies let you route to a cheaper/faster model if p99 risk is high. that's part of graceful degradation.
[14:00] Ethan: can we pin certain customers to dedicated nodes to avoid noisy neighbors?
[14:07] Samira: yes, tenant pinning is supported on Dedicated with per-tenant pools.
[14:25] Priya: during burst windows can we pre-warm kv cache with synthetic requests?
[14:33] Samira: yes, synthetic warmups are supported via preload APIs, but cost/ops need to be weighed. pre-warming works if you can predict tokens/keys to load.
[15:05] Jordan: want to dive into queueing math? we sketched M/G/k earlier, if you want detail we can follow up.
[15:12] Liam: yes please, send the modelling doc.
[15:20] Samira: will do, we'll include example sims for your trace.
[16:00] Jordan: let's talk concrete numbers - given your 1.2k qps short spike and avg 30 qps, if 90% short requests (512 tokens avg) and 10% long then you'd need roughly N GPUs (we provide spreadsheet).
[16:30] Ethan: can you ballpark N?
[16:35] Samira: rough back-of-envelope: assume an A100 can handle ~120 short requests/sec at your token sizes with low p99 when warmed, so for 1.2k qps you'd need ~10 warm gpus; long-contexts reduce concurrency so add dedicated nodes, so maybe 12-14 total with headroom. reserved baseline of 4-6, burst pool of 8-10. again we'll model exact with bench.
[17:10] Priya: ok that seems doable if cost's right. what about autoscale cooldowns - we need to avoid oscillation.
[17:22] Samira: we recommend hybrid cooldowns: quick scale-out (fast add from burst pool) but slower scale-in with hysteresis and utilization smoothing over 5-10 minutes. also use scheduled scaling for known windows to avoid churn.
[18:00] Liam: do you support eviction policies for cache when nodes scale down? we can't lose session context abruptly.
[18:12] Samira: we have graceful drain: new requests redirect, existing requests finish, and you can snapshot kv cache for fast reload. full snapshot restores are slower but possible.
[18:40] Jordan: question from our internal notes - any hard limits in private deployment for number of nodes in a pool?
[18:50] Samira: depends on customer's infra; no hard software limit but operationally we size by network and storage limits. we'll include a checklist for on-prem sizing.
[19:20] Ethan: security question - during burst to a shared pool are logs or data ever exposed?
[19:30] Jordan: no, shared burst fleet uses tenant isolation at the runtime layer; data is isolated and KV is not shared across tenants. for sensitive customers we recommend dedicated burst nodes inside their VPC.
[20:05] Priya: what's the recommended policy for retries and backpressure to maintain p99 for critical paths?
[20:15] Samira: critical paths: direct to realtime lane, strict timeouts (e.g., 300ms), avoid retries for those. less-critical: bulk with backoff. also implement client-side queuing and rate-limiting per-user.
[21:00] Ethan: any gotchas with model quantization and batching interplay?
[21:10] Samira: yes - quantized kernels may prefer smaller batch sizes to avoid precision issues; some quantized kernels do better with specific batch alignment. we'll provide kernel-specific guidance.
[21:45] Jordan: real quick, for benching we'll need your prompt set and traffic trace. you mentioned you'll share that?
[21:53] Ethan: yes we can export sample traces and top 500 prompts.
[22:05] Samira: great. we'll run a 24-hour sim with a mix and a 2-hour focused spike test. results will show cold-starts, p99, kv hit ratio, and cost.
[22:35] Liam: do you instrument request lineage so we can debug perf regressions?
[22:42] Jordan: yes trace ids, per-token timing, and we emit spans can be forwarded to your tracing system.
[23:10] Priya: about legal/procurement - we'll need pricing estimates for committed capacity vs on-demand.
[23:22] Jordan: we'll produce a pricing breakdown in the sample spreadsheet, showing amortized reserved cost.
[24:00] Samira: one more technical point - for long-contexts we recommend KV-optimized instance types; those have more memory-per-socket and lower warmup.
[24:25] Ethan: can you support pinned instances for those workloads?
[24:30] Samira: yes dedicated pinning is supported.
[25:00] Jordan: OK let's recap next steps...
[25:10] Samira: action items - we'll send capacity template, bench results, quantization guidance, and scheduling options for POC.
[25:30] Ethan: we'll send traffic traces and security requirements.
[26:00] Jordan: anything else?
[26:05] Priya: one operational detail - need to ensure KMS is available in our region, can you confirm supported clouds?
[26:15] Samira: supported: AWS, GCP, Azure; we support bring-your-own-kms with HSM integration in private. we'll include region-specific notes.
[26:40] Ethan: timeline - we want a 2 week POC starting mid-March if possible.
[26:50] Jordan: we'll propose dates and confirm resource availability.
[27:10] Samira: final note on fallback: automatic fallback to smaller model reduces latency but must be validated for quality - we'll include fallback configs to tune.
[27:45] Liam: great, thanks.
[28:00] Jordan: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with docs and the bench plan.

(Transcript continues with intermittent clarifications and Q&A, timestamps every ~30-90s)
[30:00] Samira: quick example: if you allow up to 50ms batching window, you may see 10-15% latency increase for small requests but 30-40% throughput improvement. it's a cost/latency knob.
[32:15] Ethan: are there any examples of customers using scheduled pre-warm for predictable spikes?
[32:25] Jordan: yes, finance customers pre-warm for month-end report runs - we provision burst nodes 30 minutes ahead and warm with synthetic prefixes.
[34:00] Priya: do you support custom autoscale rules (e.g., scale on kv cache miss ratio)?
[34:10] Samira: yes you can define custom metrics and scale on them, including cache hit ratio or queue depth.
[35:50] Ethan: what about instrumentation overhead - does detailed tracing add latency?
[35:58] Jordan: negligible, tracing is async; per-token timers are lightweight.
[37:20] Samira: on the bench we'll include p50/p95/p99 and cold-start distribution so you can see worst-case tails.
[39:00] Ethan: ok looking forward to the spreadsheet.
[39:10] Jordan: we'll also include recommended reserved/burst split and a cost sensitivity analysis.
[40:30] Priya: thanks team. any compliance red flags for private?
[40:40] Samira: none interiorly; we have SOC2 + ISO docs and will share our on-prem checklist.
[42:00] Liam: question - can the burst pool use different instance types for cost optimization?
[42:08] Samira: yes, you can mix instance types in pools; routing will consider latency and cost and pick compatible kernels.
[43:20] Ethan: okay if we choose too small reserved pool and rely on burst heavily does that create cost volatility?
[43:30] Jordan: yes cost variability increases with on-demand usage; the spreadsheet models worst-case vs expected.
[45:00] Samira: final wrapping notes: we'll include quantization caveats, kernel compatibility table, and recommended cooldown settings.
[46:10] Ethan: thanks all.
[46:25] Jordan: thanks folks, we'll follow up.
[46:40] (call ends)
